traveler: Arthur Ben (the name the corpus uses; his legal name stands in the VVAW obituary cited throughout and is kept out of the atlas prose)
title: Selma, the Gulf of Tonkin, and the Apron: a drafted sailor, a union librarian, and a memory theatre folded out of bed sheets
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: All Saints' Chapel, Sewanee: the birth on the plateau
stops.date_confidence: attested: the VVAW obituary gives 28 August 1947 and Sewanee, Tennessee. The pin is All Saints' Chapel, the fixed point of the town, and not a hospital of record; no birth institution is named anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: He is born on the twenty-eighth of August 1947, the first of four children in a Sewanee family. The town is not a town so much as a holding of the University of the South, an Episcopal college whose sandstone quadrangles and chapel spire run the length of a ridge on the Cumberland Plateau. He grows up inside the bell towers and the academic processions. The Anglican ritual comes to him decades before he learns to distrust the wars his country wages. Seventy-six years later his ashes come back up this mountain.
suggested_refs: All Saints' Chapel and the Domain of the University of the South, Sewanee, Tennessee

stops.name: Indian Springs School, the pines outside Birmingham
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed placement: the obituary names Sewanee Public School and then Indian Springs School but gives no years. 1959 stands for the start of a boarding-school span that must end in 1964, when he enters the University of the South.
stops.campa: After Sewanee's public school the family sends him to Indian Springs School outside Birmingham, a college-preparatory boarding school set among Alabama pines. Among the sons of the Alabama establishment, a boy raised inside the University of the South's cloister meets the harder state beyond it. He makes Eagle Scout here. Selma lies in this same state, ninety miles to the southwest, and he crosses its bridge past Alabama state troopers before he is out of his teens. The state that schools him is the state he first marches against.
suggested_refs: Indian Springs School, 190 Woodward Drive, Indian Springs Village, Shelby County, Alabama

stops.name: University of the South, the year he skips ahead
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1964 and for the university; the month is a placement at the start of term. The obituary's skipped senior year is high school, not college, and it says nothing whatever about whether he finished a degree here. An earlier research pass misread this and had him leaving Sewanee early; that reading is withdrawn.
stops.campa: He skips his senior year of high school and enters the University of the South in 1964, on the same campus that raised him, now a student rather than a faculty child. He joins Sigma Nu. The obituary that fixes this year lists four later institutions and says nothing about a degree taken here, so the atlas says nothing either. Within six months he is on an Alabama highway behind Martin Luther King, and within a year he is drafted into a Navy that keeps him four years.
suggested_refs: University of the South registrar records and Sigma Nu chapter rolls, 1964-1968

stops.name: Edmund Pettus Bridge, Selma: the crossing
stops.date_confidence: the march is attested by the obituary; the day is not. 21 March 1965 is the start of the completed walk, and his presence on any particular day of that month is reconstruction. The obituary does not say which of the three attempted marches he joined.
stops.campa: In March 1965 he walks the Selma to Montgomery march with Dr. Martin Luther King, crossing the bridge where state troopers beat marchers bloody weeks earlier on the day the country learns to call Bloody Sunday. He is seventeen, a white Tennessean out of an Episcopal college town, on Alabama asphalt for the Voting Rights Act, months before his draft notice comes. No traveler in this atlas has stood on this bridge before him. The pin is new to the corpus, and this is the earliest political act anyone records of him.
stops.quote: he took part in the March from Selma to Montgomery led by Dr. Martin Luther King
suggested_refs: The Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail and the March 1965 marcher rosters

stops.name: Alabama State Capitol, Montgomery: the end of the road
stops.date_confidence: the march's arrival at Montgomery on 25 March 1965 is public record; his own presence at the end of it follows from the obituary's word that he marched, and is not separately attested.
stops.campa: The march ends at the Alabama State Capitol, where Governor George Wallace refuses to meet the marchers and the crowd hears King from the steps instead. Fifty-four miles of highway lie behind them. Within months he is drafted, and trades the cadence of a civil rights march for the cadence of a warship. Both are columns of men walking in step, and both belong to the same year of his life. He fights the war, then spends the next fifty-nine years opposing it.
suggested_refs: The steps of the Alabama State Capitol, 25 March 1965
sources: Public historical record of the Selma to Montgomery march

stops.name: Naval Station Great Lakes, the recruit pipeline
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source names his training station. Great Lakes is where the large majority of enlisted sailors of 1965 passed, and the date is a placement inside the year of his draft, which the obituary does attest.
stops.campa: Drafted in 1965, he most likely reports to Naval Station Great Lakes on the shore of Lake Michigan, the boot camp through which most enlisted sailors of the period pass. Nothing names his station; the reconstruction rests on the standard pipeline for a drafted man who comes out the far end rated an electronics technician. Recruit training plus the technician's school runs the better part of a year, which is why he cannot have been aboard for the deployment that sails in June.
suggested_refs: Recruit training and Electronics Technician 'A' school records, US Navy, 1965-1966
sources: VVAW obituary, vvaw.org/veteran/article/?id=4301 (draft and enlistment only)

stops.name: Naval Base San Diego, the homeport
stops.date_confidence: the ship's homeport is attested, San Diego from her arrival on 11 September 1964 until the move to Norfolk in early 1974. His date of joining her is not attested anywhere; 1966 is a placement built on the training timeline.
stops.campa: USS Richmond K. Turner keeps San Diego as her homeport for the whole of his service. She is DLG-20, a guided missile frigate and destroyer leader; the Navy will not redesignate her a cruiser until 1975, a year after she has left this coast and five after he has left her. He joins her here, an electronics technician among a missile crew screening the carriers of the Seventh Fleet, and sails from these piers for the Western Pacific. The obituary names ship and rating and gives no dates at all.
stops.quote: eventually serving two tours in Vietnam as an electronics technician aboard the Richmond K. Turner
suggested_refs: USS Richmond K. Turner (DLG-20) muster rolls, National Archives at College Park

stops.name: Pearl Harbor, the refuelling stop
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source places him ashore on Oahu. San Diego based Seventh Fleet units of the 1960s customarily transited and refuelled here, and the date follows the ship's departure for her 15 October 1966 deployment.
stops.campa: Ships bound west from San Diego stop at Pearl Harbor to fuel before the long Pacific crossing to the waters off Vietnam. No document puts him ashore on Oahu. The stop is reconstructed from the transit pattern of the fleet he served in, and the atlas offers it as routine rather than as record. It is the first of the Pacific crossings he makes and remakes over two tours. He is nineteen. He has already walked from Selma to Montgomery, and now he is going to the war.
suggested_refs: Deck logs of Seventh Fleet units transiting Pearl Harbor, 1966-1968

stops.name: Subic Bay, Olongapo: the forward port
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Subic Bay is the fleet's principal forward repair, resupply, and liberty port for Vietnam operations, and a call is likely on at least one of his two tours. No document names him at Olongapo, and the date is a placement inside the 1966-67 deployment.
stops.campa: Subic Bay on Luzon is the forward repair, resupply, and liberty port for every Seventh Fleet ship working off Vietnam. The deployment pattern makes a call here likely on at least one of his two tours, and no document in his own record names the town. Ashore in Olongapo the war takes the form of bars and tailors and money changers, and the men come back down to the boats at the end of liberty and go north again to the Gulf of Tonkin, which lies some eight hundred miles across the South China Sea.
suggested_refs: Subic Bay Naval Base port visit logs, Seventh Fleet, 1966-1968

stops.name: Yankee Station, the Gulf of Tonkin
stops.date_confidence: his two Vietnam tours aboard this ship are attested; which deployments they were is not. The ship's WestPac deployments are 4 Jun to 18 Dec 1965, 15 Oct 1966 to 28 Mar 1967, Jun to Dec 1968, and Jan to Aug 1970; a man drafted in 1965 cannot have made the first. Yankee Station itself moved in April 1966 from 16N 110E to 17 30N 108 30E, and the pin uses the later position.
stops.campa: The ship works the Search and Rescue Destroyer Unit in the Gulf of Tonkin, screening the carriers at Yankee Station and pulling downed aviators out of the water. He sits inside the radar and the communications gear that guide those recoveries, the man in the steel room who hears everything and is authorised to understand none of it. The obituary states two tours in Vietnam aboard this ship and stops there. Her deployments are documented to the day. His are not documented at all.
suggested_refs: Search and Rescue Destroyer Unit records, Yankee Station, 1966-1968
sources: USS Richmond K. Turner ship history, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Richmond_K._Turner

stops.name: Off Da Nang, the coast of the war
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the deployment pattern of ships of her type, which routinely worked the coastal waters off Da Nang. The obituary logs two tours with no itinerary and places him nowhere ashore; the date sits inside the June to December 1968 deployment.
stops.campa: Ships of her type work the coastal waters off Da Nang, supporting carrier air operations and screening the lanes that feed the base. His second tour plausibly includes time in this water. Nothing places him ashore. He sees the country he will spend fifty-five years arguing about from a deck, at the distance a missile frigate keeps from a beach. The opposition takes organised form later, in Vietnam Veterans Against the War and then in Veterans for Peace.
suggested_refs: Vietnam-era deployment records for guided missile frigates off I Corps
sources: VVAW obituary, vvaw.org/veteran/article/?id=4301 (two tours, no itinerary)

stops.name: Swarthmore College, the Quaker campus
stops.date_confidence: attested: the obituary gives the 1972 graduation. The month is a placement at commencement, and no matriculation year is given.
stops.campa: In 1972, seven years after his draft notice, he graduates from Swarthmore College outside Philadelphia, a small Quaker school known for its intensity and its pacifism. The service that once interrupted an education now precedes it entirely. He arrives already a veteran, carrying two tours of a war onto a campus built on the tradition of refusing them. Every degree of his life comes after the Navy, and this is the first. The earlier version of this journey had the order reversed.
stops.quote: he graduated from Swarthmore College (1972), then earned a BA (later an MA) from Keble College of Oxford University in 1974, followed in 1978 by an ABD in English and an MLS from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
suggested_refs: Swarthmore College commencement programme, 1972

stops.name: Keble College, Oxford: the brick quadrangle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the BA and 1974; the month is a placement. No subject, tutor, or matriculation year is given in any reachable source, and the corpus description of him as a medievalist is family testimony only.
stops.campa: He crosses to England and takes his BA at Keble College in 1974, a Victorian brick quadrangle on Parks Road a world away from the sandstone chapel of his birth. Oxford deepens what his family will later remember in him, a working interest in manuscripts, knots, and old texts. He comes back to America still four years from the degree that will actually make his living, and fourteen from the building he will spend his whole working life inside. No reachable source names the subject he read here.
suggested_refs: Keble College, Parks Road, Oxford, and its matriculation registers for the early 1970s

stops.name: Oxford, the MA conferred by seniority
stops.date_confidence: the obituary's own parenthesis, a BA later an MA, marks the Oxford MA as conferred by seniority rather than examined. The year is a placement at the usual interval and is not attested. An earlier research pass folded the MA into the 1974 BA; that conflation is withdrawn.
stops.campa: The Oxford MA is not read for. It arrives by seniority some years after the BA, a formality of the place rather than a second course of study, and the obituary's parenthesis says as much. It is the one degree of his life that asks nothing of him. No source gives the year, and the atlas puts it at the usual interval and says so. This is the atlas's canonical Oxford pin, shared with John Locke, with Roger Bacon in the thirteenth century, and with Tolkien for a working lifetime. The atlas keeps the pin exactly where it has always stood and moves only the date.
suggested_refs: The Oxford MA by seniority, and the university's degree conferral registers

stops.name: Wilson Library, Chapel Hill: the pivot to the stacks
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1978, the ABD in English, and the MLS; the month is a placement. No dissertation subject, supervisor, or department beyond the word English survives in any reachable record.
stops.campa: By 1978 he is at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, all but dissertation in English and finishing instead a Master of Library Science. No thesis title and no supervisor survives in any reachable record. The pivot from Oxford medievalism to cataloguing and systems sets the next forty-five years: computer systems officer rather than professor of literature. He is thirty. The trade he will practise for the rest of his working life has a name now, and it is not the one Oxford gave him.
suggested_refs: UNC Chapel Hill School of Library Science records, class of 1978

stops.name: Miller Memorial Library, Hamden: the first machines
stops.date_confidence: attested for the post and the year 1980; the month is a placement, and the obituary gives no end date for the Hamden appointment.
stops.campa: He takes his first library post as computer systems librarian at the Hamden Public Library in Connecticut, two years out of Chapel Hill. A small New England system gives him his first charge over the machines that catalogue and retrieve. It is the same work he will do on a far larger scale within four years and for thirty-nine after that. The building stands on Dixwell Avenue and most of its borrowers walk past the room where it happens. The career that starts here runs unbroken to 2023.
suggested_refs: Miller Memorial Central Library, 2901 Dixwell Avenue, Hamden, Connecticut
sources: Nominatim geocode, Miller Memorial Central Library

stops.name: Queens College, the arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1984 and for the appointment; the month is a placement. This stop replaces the previous journey file's entire Sewanee career segment, which located his working life and a chief librarianship at the duPont Library on the mountain where he was born.
stops.campa: In 1984 he joins Queens College of the City University of New York as an assistant professor, and later teaches in the college's Graduate School of Library and Information Studies. The previous version of this journey put his working life at Sewanee, at the duPont Library, on the mountain of his birth. It was wrong. Sewanee is his birthplace and will be his grave. New York is where he works, for thirty-nine years, until he retires at seventy-five.
stops.quote: In 1984 he joined the staff at Queens College of the City University of New York (CUNY), as an assistant professor and later taught at the college's Graduate School of Library and Information Studies.
suggested_refs: Queens College CUNY faculty and staff directories, 1984-2023

stops.name: New York City, the marriage to Priscilla Murolo
stops.date_confidence: the marriage is attested by the obituary, which gives no date and no place at all. 1985 and New York are a placement inside the Queens College years and are not a finding. The previous journey file dated a marriage to 1985 at Sewanee and named no wife; the year is inherited, the place and the name are corrected.
stops.campa: He marries Priscilla Murolo, a labor historian. The obituary names her and gives neither date nor place, so the atlas sets the stop in the city where his working life runs and says out loud that it is doing so. The marriage brings him two stepsons. Sixteen years from now the two of them write a history of American labor together, and revise it seventeen years after that, in the last years of his working life. Her field and his union work are the same subject approached from two desks.
suggested_refs: New York State marriage index, searchable only under his legal name

stops.name: Benjamin S. Rosenthal Library, the electronic backbone
stops.date_confidence: attested: the library opens in 1988 and he moves into administration as its computer systems officer with the opening. The month is a placement at the start of the academic year.
stops.campa: The Rosenthal Library opens on campus in 1988 and he moves from the faculty into administration as its computer systems officer, the post he holds until retirement. Generations of Queens College students pass through a building whose electronic spine he builds and tends. This is the longest chapter of his life, longer than his childhood, his war, and all four of his schools laid end to end. He keeps a library running for thirty-five years before he folds one out of bed sheets.
suggested_refs: Benjamin S. Rosenthal Library, Queens College, Flushing, New York, opened 1988

stops.name: The New Press, Manhattan: the weekend book
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book, the co-authorship, the 2001 publication and the 2018 revision. The pin is the publisher's Manhattan address and stands for the book, not for a place he worked; the obituary names no writing address.
stops.campa: With Priscilla Murolo he co-authors an illustrated history of labor in the United States, published by The New Press in 2001 and revised in 2018. The title is a bar-room argument set in type: the weekend was not given, it was won. He is not a labor historian by training or by post. He writes it beside a wife who is one, and beside a day job keeping a university library's computers running, and the union work it draws on is his own, carried on one campus in Flushing across four decades.
stops.quote: From the Folks Who Brought You the Weekend: An Illustrated History of Labor in the United States
stops.quote_source: Book title as cited in the VVAW obituary, vvaw.org/veteran/article/?id=4301
suggested_refs: Priscilla Murolo and A. B. Chitty, From the Folks Who Brought You the Weekend (The New Press, 2001; rev. 2018)

stops.name: Queens College, the committee that meets monthly
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2006 and for the founding of the committee, which the obituary says convenes monthly. The month is a placement; no meeting room is named.
stops.campa: He founds the Queens College Unions Joint Committee on Quality of Work Life, and it convenes every month. A joint committee of the unions on one campus is not a famous thing. It is the machinery by which a workplace is argued into being habitable. He builds it, and then he shows up to it, month after month, for the seventeen years of working life he has left. He is fifty-eight. He has been walking into other people's arguments on his own time since he was seventeen and on the road to Montgomery.
suggested_refs: Professional Staff Congress chapter records, Queens College, from 2006

stops.name: Kiely Hall, Queens College: the Unsung Hero
stops.date_confidence: the award and its month, March 2011, are attested. The venue is not: Kiely Hall is inference, and the pin is best read as the Queens College campus generally. An earlier pass tagged this stop as attested while its own source line conceded the venue was reconstructed.
stops.campa: In March 2011 New York State United Teachers, parent union of the Professional Staff Congress, gives him its Unsung Hero award for his organising at Queens College. He has been a grassroots representative and never an officer. What the union is honouring is the sort of work that leaves no trace in any record: the meeting attended, the grievance carried, the committee kept alive between one contract and the next. It is the only award of his life that any source names.
stops.quote: he was honored by the PSC's parent union, NY State United Teachers, which gave him its "Unsung Hero" award in March 2011
suggested_refs: NYSUT Unsung Hero award citations, March 2011

stops.name: Queens College, the retirement after thirty-nine years
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2023; the month is a placement at the end of the academic year. The obituary gives the year of retirement and no day.
stops.campa: He retires in 2023, thirty-nine years after walking in as an assistant professor. He is seventy-five years old, and the war he sailed to has been over for half a century. The Rosenthal Library he wired has been running for thirty-five of those years, and the committee he founded still meets. He gets eight months of it. By February he is a patient at Calvary Hospital in the Bronx, and the obituary that records the retirement gives the year and not the day.
suggested_refs: Queens College retirement notices, 2023

stops.name: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial, Washington
stops.date_confidence: the dedication date is attested for the wall and not for him. No source places him at any particular Washington action, and this stop stands for the pattern of lobbying days and demonstrations his decades of membership imply.
stops.campa: The wall is dedicated on the thirteenth of November 1982, fifty-eight thousand names cut into black granite below the level of the ground, the generation he sailed with. Veterans for Peace and VVAW bring people to Washington for lobbying days and demonstrations across the decades of his membership. No source puts him here on any given date. The atlas pins the place and states plainly that the date belongs to the memorial and not to the man standing somewhere in its crowds.

stops.name: Union Square, the chapter and the paper
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the obituary attests decades of membership in VVAW and Veterans for Peace and numerous articles in The Veteran, and names no meeting hall, no demonstration, and no date. Union Square stands for a documented pattern with an undocumented venue, and the year is arbitrary within that span.
stops.campa: As a New York member of Vietnam Veterans Against the War and of Veterans for Peace he goes to chapter meetings and demonstrations in this city rather than to a national office that has shifted between Chicago and elsewhere over the decades. His chapter is named for Clarence Fitch, a combat Marine and VVAW's East Coast coordinator, dead in 1990. No single hall is named in the record. What is named is the output: numerous articles in The Veteran, across forty years.
stops.quote: He was a leader in the anti-war movement as a member of both Vietnam Veterans Against the War and Veterans for Peace and published numerous articles in VVAW's newspaper, The Veteran

stops.name: Panama City, Casco Viejo: the delegation before the invasion
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for him, attested for the mission. VVAW's own newspaper places Pete Zastrow of the National Office in Panama at the end of November 1989, and a Panamanian eyewitness thanks VVAW for having been at their side before the invasion. No published source names Arthur Ben there; his participation rests on family testimony alone. Clarence Fitch, named by an earlier pass, is linked to no Panama mission by any source and has been removed.
stops.campa: In the months before the December invasion he travels to Panama with a VVAW solidarity delegation, to watch the confrontation between Washington and Manuel Noriega and to meet Panamanian civilians opposed to intervention. His family says so. VVAW's own newspaper says the delegation existed: Pete Zastrow of the National Office writes of being in Panama at the end of November, and a Panamanian writer thanks the organisation for standing beside them. Two of those claims are published. The third is a family's word.
stops.quote: When I was in Panama at the end of November...

stops.name: Panama City, the invasion
stops.date_confidence: attested: the United States invades Panama on 20 December 1989 and removes Manuel Noriega. His own presence in the country belongs to the autumn and is not attested at all; nothing places him here in December.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of December the United States invades, removes Manuel Noriega, and ends the confrontation the delegation had gone to observe. Noriega surrenders at the Apostolic Nunciature in January, passes from American custody to French in 2010, and waits in this atlas's queue for a journey of his own. The previous version of this file had the two men meeting at Fort Gulick in 1966, on no evidence whatever. That guess is gone. A shared city, twenty-three years later, is what survives it.

stops.name: Christ Church, Bronxville: the parish
stops.date_confidence: the obituary says only that he attended Christ Church Bronxville. Residence in or near the town is inference from the parish and is not attested; an earlier pass tagged it as attested, wrongly. The year is a placement in his late New York decades.
stops.campa: The obituary names Christ Church, Bronxville, as his parish, and says nothing at all about where he and Priscilla Murolo lived. The atlas will not turn a church into an address. The Sewanee-born son of an Episcopal college town ends in another Episcopal nave, in the northern suburbs of the city where he has worked since 1984. Bronxville sits about six miles north of the hospital where he dies. Where he slept for forty years is not on the record at all.

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, the Bronx: the sheets folded
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the hospice material is corpus-internal family memory from the locked essay 200_arthur_ben.md and is not publicly citable. January 2024 is a placement inside the weeks before his attested death on 11 February 2024.
stops.campa: In the hospice room his hands work the bedsheets in a fixed sequence, vertical then horizontal, doubling and doubling again, the same motion the children watched him make on a tablecloth for years. The family reads it late: a control panel laid out in linen for a memory theatre, in which archives are filed and retrieved, relics are placed, and banquets are set with care for the order of placement. He operates it from the bed until his hands give out.
stops.quote: His sequencing of vertical and horizontal doubling of the cloth created a mantle which formed the control panel of a complex memory theatre.
stops.quote_source: 200_arthur_ben.md, locked essay corpus, not publicly citable
suggested_refs: Frances Yates, The Art of Memory, on the theatre as an operable instrument
sources: VVAW obituary, vvaw.org/veteran/article/?id=4301 (place and date of death)

stops.name: Bab al-Mandab, the gate of tears named from the bed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and flatly contradicted by the service record. The strait is named by the dying man in family testimony. USS Richmond K. Turner was a Pacific Fleet ship homeported at San Diego throughout his service, and her only documented Suez transit is April 1991, so no vessel of his attested record went near this water. The atlas states the contradiction and leaves it open.
stops.campa: The Red Sea narrows to eighteen miles between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, and the strait is called the Gate of Tears for the ships it has taken. He names it from the hospice bed, alongside the tribes of Yemen and of Gaul. Ibn Battuta came down this water in 1330 bound for Aden. Abu Karib ruled the Himyarites on the Yemeni shore and, in the Arab tradition, first draped the Kaaba in cloth. How a San Diego frigate put him here, no record explains and nobody in the room asks.
stops.quote: Amidst his flickering, Ben spoke of his travels through the Straits of Bab al-Mandan and Malacca, the tribes of Yemen and Gaul, and the bloodlines of Abraham.
stops.quote_source: 200_arthur_ben.md, the hospice room, locked essay corpus, not publicly citable
suggested_refs: The Bab al-Mandab strait between Perim and the Djibouti shore
sources: USS Richmond K. Turner ship history (the contradiction)

stops.name: The Strait of Malacca, the narrow water
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and contradicted on the same grounds as Bab al-Mandab. The strait is named in family testimony from the hospice room; a San Diego to Pearl Harbor to Subic Bay routing passes nowhere near it. The date is sequence within the last weeks and not a calendar finding.
stops.campa: Between Sumatra and the Malay peninsula the sea closes to a channel every cargo of the East has had to thread. Marco Polo waited out a monsoon on the Sumatran side in 1291; Ibn Battuta crossed to the sultanate of Samudera Pasai in 1345 and found a Shafi'i court at the end of the ocean. The dying librarian names this strait and Bab al-Mandab together, two places where the world is forced narrow and everything passing through can be counted. It is the shelving instinct applied to the sea.
suggested_refs: The Malacca strait between One Fathom Bank and Port Klang

stops.name: Mecca, the bloodlines of Abraham
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a station of the hospice speech and not a journey he made. The pin is the atlas's canonical Kaaba, inherited unchanged from the previous journey file and shared with the Abraham and Abu Karib files.
stops.campa: He speaks of the bloodlines of Abraham in the same breath as two sea straits, which is to say he files a genealogy and a shipping lane in adjacent drawers. Abraham and Ishmael raise the House at the eastern end of the water he names, and Abu Karib of Yemen is remembered as the first to clothe it. A man who once hung the Throne Verse on his children's door in Tennessee comes back at the end to the line both of his talismans descend from, the Hebrew and the Arabic together.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Genesis and Qur'anic accounts of Abraham and Ishmael

stops.name: The Temple Mount, Jerusalem: the apron and the murdered architect
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a station of the hospice speech. The pin is the canonical Temple Mount of the Hiram Abiff and Solomon files, inherited unchanged from the previous journey file.
stops.campa: Hiram Abiff dies on this platform in the Masonic legend, struck down by three of his own workmen for a word he will not give, and Solomon's house is finished without him. stops.name: Paris, the amphitheatre built for the king
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a station of the hospice speech and a structural parallel, not a place he went. The pin is the canonical Paris of the Giulio Camillo file, inherited unchanged from the previous journey file.
stops.campa: Giulio Camillo built a wooden theatre for Francis I in which the spectator stood on the stage and the seven grades of the world rose in front of him, every image a drawer holding everything sayable about its subject. Viglius inspected the thing at Venice and reported both the amazement and the drawers. Camillo died at Milan in 1544 and the theatre was never found. Four and a half centuries on, a librarian folds one out of hospital linen in the Bronx and works it with his hands.
suggested_refs: Giulio Camillo, L'Idea del Theatro (Florence, 1550)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second life told aloud
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and fictive by the essay's own framing: this is a life imagined for him at the bedside, not a life he lived. The pin is the canonical Buenos Aires of the Borges file, inherited unchanged from the previous journey file.
stops.campa: His stepson holds his hand and tells him a story about himself in which he lives in Argentina instead, in a city that puts books about books at its centre, keeps his library of arcana rather than selling it, and befriends the bookseller Raul Veroni. Borges was made director of the National Library there in 1955, by which time he could no longer read, and wrote that God had given him at once the books and the night. The second life is told aloud to the man it is about, in the room where the first is ending.
stops.quote: I had been imagining a second life for Ben, one in Argentina and the city of Buenos Aires, where libraries and literature and books about books are placed at the center.

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, the apron specified
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: corpus-internal family memory, not publicly citable, and sequence within the last weeks rather than a calendar date. The previous journey file dated this scene to March 2019 at Sewanee; the attested death of 11 February 2024 in the Bronx moves it.
stops.campa: Alone with the two boys he prompts the construction of the thing he needs for his departure. It is to be hand stitched. It is to have pockets. He describes it with the precision of a man writing a finding aid: dimensions, closure, contents, and the order of the contents. Forty-three years of describing objects for other people to retrieve, and the object described here is the man doing the describing. The family takes down the specification and begins to sew.
suggested_refs: The apron itself, if it survives in the family's keeping

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, the two front pockets
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the apron and its pockets, which are corpus-internal family memory. The interment of his own ashes at Sewanee with his parents and his brother is attested by the obituary as an intention.
stops.campa: The two pockets at the front are to hold the ashes of his parents. He was born to them on a mountain in Tennessee and means to leave carrying them at his waist, in a garment sewn by hand by his wife's sons. His own ashes are to go back up that same mountain, to lie with theirs and with his younger brother's. The garment is loaded before it is ever tied. It is a container first and a symbol second, and what it contains is the two people this atlas pinned on a mountain in its opening stop.
suggested_refs: The family plot at Sewanee, Tennessee
sources: VVAW obituary, vvaw.org/veteran/article/?id=4301 (the ashes and the family graves)

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, the knot in the likeness of Shin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: corpus-internal family memory, not publicly citable, and sequence within the last weeks rather than a calendar date.
stops.campa: The apron ties in front with a knot made in the likeness of Shin, the three-pointed crown of the Hebrew letter, the letter the priest's hands make in the blessing and the letter cut into the head of a phylactery. He tells his wife that Hebrew and Arabic writing is emerging inside his pancreas and his liver and that he cannot read what it says. The inscriptions are making a phylactery of him. A phylactery is a small box of fabric and leather with a verse shut inside it, and the man wearing one never sees the text he is carrying.

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, I need help with my strings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: corpus-internal family memory, not publicly citable, and sequence within the last weeks rather than a calendar date.
stops.campa: He reaches his arms out with a grimace and says it plainly, the way a man says a thing about equipment. The strings are in his back. His stepson slides a hand between the body and the bed and finds enormous knots between the fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae and the left shoulder. The operator of the theatre is requesting maintenance on the mechanism, and the mechanism is a spine. Nobody in the room treats the request as a figure of speech, and his stepson goes to work on the knots.

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, the lifetime membership
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance by the closing line of the obituary, which gives no date. The placement in the last days follows the obituary's own phrase, very near the end of his life.
stops.campa: Very near the end he signs up for a lifetime membership in Vietnam Veterans Against the War. He has belonged to it since the years after the Navy and has written for its newspaper across four decades; the membership buys him nothing he does not already have. He is dying, and he pays for a lifetime of something. The obituary calls it a statement of enduring solidarity and gives it the last line of his life, which is where the organisation decided it belonged.
stops.quote: Very near the end of his life, Ben signed up for a lifetime membership in VVAW, as a statement of enduring solidarity

stops.name: Calvary Hospital, the departure
stops.date_confidence: attested: the obituary gives 11 February 2024 at Calvary Hospital in the Bronx. This replaces the previous journey file's placement of his death at Sewanee in March 2019, made when no obituary had been found.
stops.campa: He dies on the eleventh of February 2024, seventy-six years old, with the apron made, the pockets loaded, and the knot tied in the shape of a letter. His wife survives him, and two stepsons, and his siblings; his parents and a younger brother went before. The tributes his comrades file in The Veteran run to a few lines each. One of them says that one of the tall timbers has fallen. Four men write, and none of them writes at length. The paper prints the four of them under a single heading and closes the file.
stops.quote: Truly, One of the tall timbers has fallen.

stops.name: Sewanee, the ashes carried back up the mountain
stops.date_confidence: the obituary states the intention that his ashes be interred at Sewanee with those of his parents and his brother. The interment itself is not verified and no date is given; June 2024 is a placement.
stops.campa: His ashes are to be interred at Sewanee, alongside those of his parents and his brother, on the mountain where he was born seventy-six years earlier and where he had not worked a day of his adult life. The previous version of this journey had him living and dying here, chief librarian of the duPont Library, and was wrong on every count but the ground. The ground was right. He comes back to it carrying, in two stitched pockets, the people who put him there.
